passage: The generator in the college library coughed to life at three, drowning the ceiling fans in a steady roar. Nitin pushed his earplugs deeper and opened the thermodynamics notes. Exams were eight days away, and he had lost every afternoon last week to one thing: Irfan appearing at the door with a grin and a plan. So on Sunday night he had written a line inside the cover of his notebook: If Irfan asks before six, answer "later" and meet him at six. At four the door swung open. Irfan waved two tickets for the inter-college match, already started. Nitin felt the old pull in his chest. He tapped the notebook cover, then walked out to the corridor. "Later. I'm out at six, save me a spot." Irfan rolled his eyes but nodded. Nitin went back in, finished two problem sets through the generator noise, and reached the ground by quarter past six for the final overs.

qa.q: What did Nitin write inside the cover of his notebook?
qa.a: He wrote: If Irfan asks before six, answer "later" and meet him at six.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when Irfan waved the match tickets, and why did the prepared line help?
qa.a: Nitin felt a tempted pull toward the match, but because he had already decided his answer on Sunday, he didn't have to argue with himself in that tense moment.

qa.q: What could Nitin add to his plan if the generator noise made studying harder on other days?
qa.a: He could plan a second if-then, such as moving to a quieter reading room when the generator starts, so one obstacle doesn't undo the other plan 🙂

qa.q: How might Irfan see Nitin's answer at the door?
qa.a: Irfan might be a little annoyed at first, but he still gets a clear time to expect Nitin, which is kinder than a vague maybe.

grounding: It shows a student who pre-planned a response to a friend's invitation during study hours, so the intention held despite the pull and the noise.

passage: Parveen's phone buzzed on the long wooden table of the municipal library in Pune. Uma: "Sale at the market near FC Road!! Coming?? 🛍️" Parveen smiled and did not open the chat yet. Taped to her pencil box was a yellow slip she had written after a wasted Tuesday: Uma calls before six → "Six, at the chai stall." She had noticed that every time she answered in the moment, she argued herself into going. Now she only had to copy the slip. She typed, "Six, at the chai stall 🙂 saving my brain for this chapter first." A crying-laughing reply came, then "fine, six sharp." Parveen turned back to the accounts chapter, the one she had avoided for days. At five-fifty she closed the book with two exercises done and walked out to the stall, where Uma was already holding two cutting chais.

qa.q: What was written on the yellow slip taped to Parveen's pencil box?
qa.a: The slip said: Uma calls before six → "Six, at the chai stall."

qa.q: Why did Parveen feel relieved to have the slip ready when Uma's message came?
qa.a: She felt relieved because she knew she usually argued herself into going when she decided in the moment; the slip meant she only had to copy an answer she had already chosen.

qa.q: What small step would help Parveen keep this plan working?
qa.a: She could keep the slip where she studies every day and update it if new distractions appear, like a group chat, with the same 'later, at six' reply.

qa.q: If you were Uma, what would you want from Parveen's reply?
qa.a: As Uma, I'd want a clear time rather than a no, so the friendship still feels wanted; getting 'six, at the chai stall' does that 😊

grounding: It shows a student using a pre-written if-then reply to a friend's invitation during study hours, which kept her studying and still meeting the friend at six.

passage:
"Aadhya! Riddhi's cake is at three in Block C, everyone's going."
"Uma, it's two-forty. Remember what I told you on Monday?"
"The 'later, six o'clock' thing? I thought you were joking."
"I wasn't. If someone invites me during study hours, I say later and I come at six. That's the whole rule."
"It's a birthday, not a film."
"I know. That's exactly why I decided it in advance. If I decide now, I'll go, then stay for photos, then it's dinner and my lab record is still blank."
"So you'll miss the cake?"
"I'll come at six. Tell Riddhi to save me a slice with extra icing."
"You're so strange." Uma paused. "Okay, six. I'm holding you to it."
"Please do."
Aadhya turned back to her lab record. At six she knocked on Block C, the record finished, and found a slice wrapped in a napkin with her name on it.

qa.q: What time was Riddhi's cake cutting?
qa.a: The cake was at three in Block C.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya feel more confident saying no when she had decided the rule on Monday?
qa.a: She felt steadier because deciding in the moment usually led her to go, stay for photos and dinner; the Monday rule took the tempting choice out of the moment.

qa.q: What went well in how Aadhya handled the invitation, and what could she add?
qa.a: She kept her rule and still offered a clear time, so the friendship didn't suffer; she could also tell close friends her study hours in advance so fewer invitations clash.

qa.q: How does Uma see Aadhya's rule at first, and what changes by the end?
qa.a: At first Uma thinks it is strange or a joke, but by the end she agrees to hold Aadhya to six, becoming a helper for the plan.

grounding: It shows a student using a prepared 'later, at six' answer to a friend's invitation during study hours, which let her finish her work and still join the celebration.

passage: Pallavi, you're asking how I stay so regular with my walks? Sit, let me tell you about the year I did not. I was twenty-four then, your Manjula aunty, working at the bank in Mysuru. On the first of January I told my roommate Revathi, "This year I'll be healthier." That was all. No time, no place. I bought a yoga mat and felt wonderful for a week. Then came the audit. Some mornings I was tired, some evenings it rained, some days I just didn't feel like it. Each day I thought, I'll start properly tomorrow. By February the mat was rolled up under the cot with dust on it, and I was eating fried snacks at the tea shop again. Revathi never teased me, but she stopped asking. It was only the next year, when I said "after the bus drops me, I walk around the lake," that anything stuck.

qa.a: She bought a yoga mat.

qa.a: Revathi may have felt awkward or unsure whether to mention it, so she stopped asking to avoid hurting Manjula.

passage: Trisha wrote it on the whiteboard of the flat on New Year's morning: EAT BETTER. MOVE MORE. Madhav, her flatmate, added a smiley. Then the night-shift rota at the call centre changed. Some weeks she started at nine at night, some at eleven, and the canteen shut at midnight. Whenever she remembered the whiteboard, she was either asleep or on a break with ten minutes and a vending machine. "I'll plan it when the rota settles," she told Madhav in the third week. It didn't settle. On the first Sunday of February, Madhav found her at the counter with a cup of instant noodles at four in the afternoon, her breakfast. The whiteboard still said MOVE MORE, the letters faded where her sleeve had brushed them. "I did mean it," she said, not looking up. "I just never decided what it actually meant on a Tuesday night."

qa.q: What did Trisha write on the whiteboard on New Year's morning?
qa.a: She wrote EAT BETTER. MOVE MORE.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling when she said she never decided what the goal meant on a Tuesday night?

grounding: It shows an adult whose vague resolution, made without a when or how and squeezed by shift work, faded back into old routines by February.

passage: "So, still on the healthy year?" Bhavna asked, holding the lift door on the fourth floor of their Hyderabad office. Afreen laughed and stepped in. On January first she had announced it at Bhavna's rooftop party: this year, I'm getting healthier. Everyone had clapped. In the first week she had taken the stairs twice and gone to bed early once. After that the days just filled up. Some nights she scrolled until one, some mornings she grabbed a samosa from the canteen because she was running late. None of it felt like breaking a promise, because the promise had never said anything specific. Now it was the second week of February, and she was in the lift again. "I'm still on it," Afreen said. "Sort of." As the lift climbed, she tried to name one thing she had actually changed and couldn't find one.

qa.q: Where did Afreen announce her plan to get healthier?
qa.a: She announced it at Bhavna's rooftop party on January first.

qa.q: Why didn't Afreen feel she was breaking a promise when she scrolled late or grabbed a samosa?
qa.a: Because the promise never said anything specific, each slip felt harmless; by February she felt uneasy and a little embarrassed when she couldn't name one real change.

qa.q: What would you advise Afreen to try instead of 'getting healthier'?
qa.a: Pick one specific action tied to a clear cue, for example taking the stairs whenever she arrives at the office, so it happens without needing mood or memory.

qa.q: What would change if Afreen had said 'I take the stairs every morning' at the party?
qa.a: She would have a clear moment each day to act and to notice a slip, and Bhavna could have asked about something concrete instead of a vague goal.

grounding: It shows an adult whose resolution to be healthier said nothing about when or how, so ordinary busy days pulled her back to old habits by February.

subtype: Attaching a new action to an existing cue [Response]
passage:
Dear Jasleen,

You asked how the stretching is going since our yoga classes ended. Honestly? Better than when I had a class to go to.

For months I kept telling myself, stretch in the evening. Every evening I'd sit on the sofa and debate: now, after dinner, after this episode. Usually the debate won.

Then I tried something small. I brush my teeth every night without thinking, so I decided the stretch comes right after. Toothbrush goes in the cup, I step onto the bathroom mat, I do the hamstring stretch and the doorframe stretch. Five slow breaths each.

There's no decision anymore. Last Thursday I came home from a wedding at midnight, brushed, and was halfway through the doorframe stretch before I remembered I was tired.

My back thanks you for the push in class.

Joseph

qa.q: What does Joseph do right after putting the toothbrush in the cup?
qa.a: Joseph steps onto the bathroom mat and does the hamstring stretch and the doorframe stretch.

qa.q: How does Joseph feel about stretching now compared with the evening debates?
qa.a: Joseph feels relieved and a little amused; the old evening debate felt exhausting, but now the stretch just follows brushing, so there's nothing to argue about.

qa.q: What could Jasleen take from Joseph's letter for a new habit?
qa.a: Jasleen could pick an existing daily routine, like making morning tea, and attach the new action right after it so it starts without deciding.

qa.q: How might Jasleen feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Jasleen will likely feel pleased and proud that the push in class led somewhere, and happy to hear from a former classmate

grounding: It shows an adult who tied stretching to the stable cue of brushing teeth, so it now begins without deliberation.

subtype: Attaching a new action to an existing cue [Response]
passage: Disha, you want the secret? It isn't willpower, I promise you. I drive a delivery van for a bakery in Kochi, eight hours in that seat, and by last year my lower back was complaining every evening. The physio at the clinic showed me three stretches. For weeks I did them exactly never. I'd think, after tea, after the news, then I'd fall asleep. What changed was stupid and small. I already brush my teeth every morning at five-fifteen, no matter what. So I said, the moment I rinse, I stretch. Right there by the sink. Now my hands put the toothbrush down and my body just bends. Last month I went to my cousin's village for a funeral, different house, different sink, and I still did it, because brushing came with me. So that's my secret, Disha, from Jeevan the van man: glue it to something you already never miss.

passage: Study hour at the girls' hostel began at seven sharp, with the warden's bell and forty chairs scraping at once. Across the table, Sabina tapped her own ear and raised an eyebrow. Shalini sighed, pulled the earphones out, and wrapped them around the phone. The room became chairs creaking and pages turning. She started the passage again.

Hi Ayesha,

Ammi says you're struggling to start homework in Class 9, so here's something I've been doing since the summer. Don't laugh.

I made a playlist of my favourite songs, the good ones, and I only play them while doing homework. Not on the bus, not while gaming. So when it's homework time there's actually something I want. It made starting so much easier 😊. Diagrams, maps, copying notes, all fine.

But I found out the hard way it doesn't work for everything. Last week I did physics numericals with the songs on and got half of them wrong, silly mistakes, because I was humming instead of thinking. Now I do the playlist for the easy stuff and total quiet for problems.

Try it and tell me what you'd put on yours.

Your cousin, Jeevan

Honestly it worked like magic. I'd come home, think about the songs, and suddenly I wanted to sit at my desk. Geography maps, English grammar, I was flying. Dear Nikita,

You asked how I'm surviving hostel life without Mummy doing my clothes. The truth is, I've made a small bargain with myself.

You know how I love that detective podcast? I only let myself listen to it while I'm doing laundry or out on my run. Nowhere else. Not in bed, not in the mess.

At first it felt silly. But now on Sunday mornings I actually want to haul the bucket to the wash area, because episode twelve is waiting. Last week I washed, rinsed and hung everything before the episode even ended, then went for a run to hear the finish.

My roommate thinks I'm crazy for looking forward to laundry. My clothes and my legs disagree.

Tell Papa I'm eating properly.

Your bhaiya,
Nilesh

passage: Kwame had three weeks to write the history essay on his family's migration from Kumasi to London. Mr Emil, his teacher, had called it the essay that would decide his predicted grade. If he tried properly and it was only average, it would prove he wasn't clever, not really. So he cleaned his football boots. He reorganised his bookshelf. He told his mum he was "gathering sources." The night before the deadline, he wrote from ten until three, without time to call his grandfather for the stories he'd planned to use. The essay came back with a B minus and a note: "Where is your grandfather's voice?" Kwame stared at it and thought, at least I didn't really try.

passage: I used to tell everyone I'm a pressure person. Put me in front of a deadline and I light up. In second year, Lavanya and I had a group report on water tariffs due Monday. She wanted to start on Wednesday. I said, relax, I'll do my half on Sunday night, that's when I'm brilliant. And honestly, the first few hours felt amazing, the tea, the silence of the hostel, my heart racing like a cricket chase. By three I was copying my own sentences twice. By five my eyes burned and I had a headache that lasted all of Monday. Lavanya read my part in the corridor and fixed two wrong numbers with a pen before we submitted. Looking back, I don't think I was brilliant that night. I think I was just awake, and scared, and calling it energy. I'm Yash, by the way, still unlearning this.

Note, Friday, hostel warden's desk

Keerthana, second-year commerce, came down to the common room at about 1 a.m. on Thursday for the third night this week, asking for hot water and the table fan. She told me cheerfully that she "only really works when the deadline is breathing on her neck." She was laughing, but her hands shook while filling the flask, and she had skipped dinner.

By 6 a.m. she was still at the table. At breakfast she mentioned she had submitted the assignment with the last section "a bit rushed" and then fell asleep in the reading room with her head on her bag.

After she woke, I sat with her and asked what she would do differently. She said she likes the rush. I suggested she try one earlier small deadline with a friend, and that she eat and see the campus nurse if the headaches keep coming. Will check with her Monday.

— Gurleen, warden

Tuesday, 11:40 p.m.

Dear diary, it's happening again and I love it a bit. Economics essay due at 9 a.m. tomorrow and I have exactly the title. Hemant texted at eight: "started?" I sent a thumbs up 👍 and went back to cricket highlights. I KNOW I work better when it's close. Last sem I wrote the best essay of my life in one night. (Did I, though? It got a B.)

12:50 a.m. Three paragraphs. Heart thumping. Chai number two. This is the good part, the buzz, when words just come.

4:10 a.m. Done. Didn't check references. Eyes burning.

Dear Madhuri,

It's been four months since our convocation, and you asked whether I've applied anywhere. The honest answer is no, and I'm writing because I can't say it out loud.

There are three paths on my desk: the master's in Delhi, the analyst job in Bengaluru, the NGO fellowship in Odisha. Each time I open a form, I think, what if this is the wrong one and I can't undo it? So I close it and research some more. It feels careful, like I'm protecting myself.

Last week the Delhi deadline passed. I didn't choose not to go. I just didn't choose, and that turned out to be the same thing.

Could we talk on Sunday? Maybe you can help me pick one to try, not the perfect one.

Love,
Sunaina

passage: Ganga akka, you asked me on the call why I'm still home in Madurai six months after graduating. Okay, so, here's the thing. I had two offers in my head: the civil engineering site job in Chennai and the government exam coaching my father wanted. Both felt huge. If I took the site job and hated it, I'd have lost a year of exam prep. If I did coaching and failed, I'd have lost the job. So I did neither. I told everyone I was "weighing it." Every morning I'd open the job portal, read the posting again, and close it. It felt responsible, honestly, like I was being careful. Then in March the Chennai company sent a polite email: the position had been filled. That's when it hit me. Weighing it was already a decision. It was just one I never actually made. That's where Deepak is now, akka. Starting over.

passage:
Monday, early June. Kashish spread the three brochures across her bed in the Jaipur flat: design school in Pune, a paid internship at a textile studio, a gap year at her aunt's weaving centre. "I'll decide this week," she told her brother Deepak, who was eating toast in the doorway.

Two weeks later, a Saturday. The brochures had moved to the desk, now under a pile of clothes. Deepak asked about the internship. "Still comparing," Kashish said, scrolling reviews on her phone. She had read each review page so many times she could quote them.

Late July, a Thursday. The internship posting had vanished from the studio's website. Kashish sat on the floor, reading the design school's email: seats full for this year. Only her aunt's offer was still open, not because she had picked it, but because it was the one without a date. "I didn't choose," she said quietly. Deepak sat down beside her.

qa.q: How many brochures did Kashish spread across her bed?
qa.a: Three brochures: design school, an internship, and a gap year at her aunt's weaving centre.

qa.q: What was Kashish feeling when she said 'I didn't choose' in late July?
qa.a: She felt stunned and regretful, realising that endless comparing, which had felt safe, had let two options close without her ever deciding.

qa.q: What could Kashish have done in June to avoid this?
qa.a: She could have set her own deadline for each option and taken one small step, like applying to the internship, while still thinking about the others.

qa.q: How does Deepak seem to experience his sister's delay?
qa.a: Deepak keeps checking in and ends up sitting beside her, which suggests he was concerned and wants to comfort her rather than blame her.

grounding: It shows a graduate whose fear of risky, irreversible choices kept her comparing until the options chose for her by default, over several weeks.

Week one, a Monday. In the reading room, Pallavi pushed her thesis folder away. "I'll start the literature review tomorrow, properly." Madhuri nodded and kept working, but noticed Pallavi's jaw was tight.

Week two, a Thursday. Same words, softer. "Tomorrow, promise." This time Pallavi left early, and later sent Madhuri a message: "I'm useless." Madhuri read it three times, a knot in her stomach, and replied with a heart.

Week three, a Tuesday. Madhuri waited by the library steps. "Sit with me for twenty minutes," she said. "Just twenty. What's the easiest piece?" Pallavi thought. "Listing the papers I've already read." They sat side by side, Madhuri on her own work, Pallavi typing titles. When the timer went off, Pallavi had a list of eleven and didn't stop. Madhuri pretended not to notice the smile.

qa.a: She had a list of eleven.

qa.a: Offering to sit together for just twenty minutes and start with the easiest piece worked, because it made starting small and less lonely.

passage: Come, sit, I'll tell you about Arnab. We were in the same hostel in Shillong, both doing botany, when I was about your age. Every evening in the mess, Arnab said the same thing: "From tomorrow I'll start the herbarium file." The next evening, again tomorrow. I noticed he ate less each time he said it, and once he just stared at his plate and said, "What's wrong with me?" I felt sorry and also a little annoyed, I won't pretend. I didn't know what to do. Then one night I said, "Arnab, bring your file. We'll sit in the common room for twenty minutes. Just press one leaf." He came, grumbling. That leaf became six. In the end he submitted before me. So when you watch a friend going round and round, remember that, beta. Lalremsiami learned it at nineteen.

qa.a: The turn came when Lalremsiami invited Arnab to sit together for twenty minutes and press just one leaf; a small, shared start broke the cycle of 'tomorrow'.

qa.a: He probably felt hopeful saying it, then worse each time it didn't happen, which showed in eating less and asking what was wrong with him.
